did_you_know.text: Did you know? The LORD commanded Isaiah to write the words “Maher-shalal-hash-baz” on a large scroll with an ordinary stylus—that is, in clear and legible writing—to provide a public witness to the prophecy.
Did you know? Isaiah was instructed to bring two trustworthy witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Jeberechiah, to confirm the prophetic inscription.
Did you know? Isaiah’s son’s name also became a prophetic sign: “Maher-shalal-hash-baz.” The name expresses how near the event prophesied by the LORD was.

Did you know? The prophecy states that before the child knows how to say “My father” and “My mother,” the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried away before the king of Assyria.
Did you know? The gently flowing waters of Shiloah symbolize quiet and moderate leadership in this chapter; the people rejected them and preferred Rezin and the son of Remaliah.
Did you know? Because the people rejected the waters of Shiloah, the king of Assyria is described as “the River”—vast and mighty waters that will overflow their banks and sweep across the land.
Did you know? Although the Assyrian flood will reach up to the neck and pass through Judah, the prophecy mentions the phrase “God is with us” within the threat, emphasizing God’s presence.
Did you know? The chapter presents “God is with us” as the answer to the nations’ plans: they may make plans and speak, but their counsel will not stand if it does not accord with God’s will.

Did you know? The LORD is described in two contrasting ways in this chapter: He can be a “sanctuary” for those who seek Him, but also a “stone of offense” and a “rock of stumbling” for those who stumble over Him.
Did you know? Isaiah rejects turning to mediums and spiritists and directs the people to seek their God; in this way, the chapter sets the law and the testimony against seeking answers from the dead.
